:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,-2):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(-1)=2(-1)+3=-2+3=1

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}$ at the point $(1,-3).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4{x}^{5/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}-10(1)^{3/2}=-7\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line  ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{7}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-5}+7x) \\  & =-10{x}^{-6}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-10(1)^{-6}+7=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}$ at the point $\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}\right).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{2}{9}.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$

$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Equation of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$

$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to $y = 4x - 1$ and passes through the point $(-8,7).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $l_1$ denote the line $y = 4x - 1,$ and let $l_2$ denote the line we want to find.

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of $l_2$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of $l_1.$ Since $l_1$ has a slope of $4,$ the line $l_2$ must have a slope of $-\dfrac{1}{4}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\dfrac{1}{4}$ and pass through the point $(x_1,y_1)=(-8,7).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_1 &= m(x-x_1) \\[5pt]
y - 7 &= -\dfrac{1}{4}(x-(-8)) \\[5pt]
y - 7 &= -\dfrac{1}{4}(x+8)\\[5pt]
y - 7 &= -\dfrac{1}{4}x - 2 \\[5pt]
y &= -\dfrac{1}{4}x + 5
	\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(3,4)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(0,1)$ and $(-2,4).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes which are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope $m_1$ of the line passing through the points $(0,1)$ and $(-2,4)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{4-1}{-2-0} \\  & =\frac{3}{-2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m \cdot \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = -1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m = \dfrac{2}{3}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(3,4).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =\frac{2}{3}(x-3) \\ y-4 & =\frac{2}{3}x-2 \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the equation of the line that passes through the point $(6,2)$ and is perpendicular to $3x-2y=1?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation $3x-2y=1$ in its slope-intercept form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2y & =1 \\ -2y & =-3x+1 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of the new line should be the negative reciprocal of the slope of the given line $y=\dfrac{3}{2}x - \dfrac{1}{2}.$ The given line has a slope of $\dfrac{3}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\dfrac{2}{3}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ and pass through the point $(x_1,y_1) = (6,2).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-6) \\ y-2 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+4 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+6\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y=3x^2+1$ where the tangent line has a slope of $-1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+1.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to $f'(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+1) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =3\cdot 2x+0 \\  & =6x+0 \\  & =6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set $f'(x) = -1$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-1 \\ 6x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $-1$ at the point where $x=-\dfrac 1 6.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + \dfrac {1}{x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^2+\dfrac 1 x.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to $f'(2).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =2\cdot x-{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =2(2)-(2{)}^{-2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\dfrac{15}{4}.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^4 + 3\sqrt [3]{x^2}$ at the point $(1,4)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
This time, we'll use $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =4\cdot {x}^{3}+3\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {x}^{-1/3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}+2{x}^{-1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =4(1{)}^{3}+2(1{)}^{-1/3} \\  & =4+2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $6.$
